title: How to add an email account in Apple Mail on Mac: steps and server settings
metaTitle: How to Add an Email Account in Apple Mail on Mac
description: How to add an email account in Apple Mail on Mac: choose Mail > Add Account, enter your address, and check server settings if sign-in fails.
targetKeyword: how to add an email account in apple mail on mac
secondaryKeywords: add gmail to apple mail mac

intro: Open Mail, choose Mail > Add Account, type your email address, and click Continue. Mail then asks for your password and other account details, and you follow the prompts until it finishes.
tldr: Open Mail and choose Mail > Add Account. Enter your full email address and click Continue.
Apple says to create the account on the provider's website before you add it to your Mac.
You can also add it in System Settings > Internet Accounts > Add Account.
To fix connection fields, go to Mail > Settings > Accounts, select the account, and click Server Settings.
Gmail uses IMAP by default. Google recommends Sign in with Google over app passwords.

stats.label: Share of tracked email opens in September 2026 that Litmus credited to Apple Mail. It counts opens, not users.

blocks.text: Adding an email account in Apple Mail takes about ten minutes when you have everything ready. Most delays come from a missing password or a server field nobody filled in. Gather the details first, then follow the steps.
What you need before you start

items: Your full email address and its current password.
The account already created on your provider's website. Apple says to do this first.
The Mail app open on your Mac, with the window active.
For Gmail, a Google account you can sign in to in a browser.
For a custom iCloud domain, your primary iCloud Mail address and the same Apple Account on each device.

blocks.text: Apple's Get Started page gives the short version: choose Mail > Add Account, enter your email address, and follow the instructions. It also says an email account is needed before you can send mail. The steps in this guide expand that line into the screens you will see.
Add the account from the Mail menu

The Mail menu only shows when Mail is the active app. Click the Mail window or its Dock icon first, then open the menu. The commands you need sit inside that menu, so you do not have to hunt for them.
Read each menu path as a sequence. Mail > Add Account means click Mail in the menu bar, then click Add Account in the list that opens. Mail > Settings > Accounts works the same way, one level deeper.
Pick your provider: iCloud, Gmail, Exchange, or another

Apple's add-account page lists four account types: iCloud, Gmail (Google), Exchange, and school, work, or other accounts. It does not name Yahoo, AOL, or Outlook. That does not mean those providers won't work. It means Apple's page doesn't cover them, so check the provider's own help pages for server details.
If Mail doesn't recognize your address, click choose from a list and select the domain. Read the provider name before you click Continue, so a work account doesn't end up set up as iCloud.
Add an account from System Settings instead

You can also start in System Settings. Open System Settings, click Internet Accounts in the sidebar, and scroll if you can't see it. Click Add Account, then enter your email address or choose from a list. Apple says to create the account on the provider's website before you start, so have that ready.
If your provider isn't listed, click Add Other Account and choose the account type. Then enter the account name, password, and any other details Apple asks for.

rows: You are already in Mail and want one more mailbox
System Settings > Internet Accounts > Add Account
You want to set the account up outside Mail, or the provider is not in Mail's list
Mail > Settings > Accounts, then make sure Mail is selected
Another app already uses the account and you want Mail to use it too
blocks.caption: Three places to add or manage an account on a Mac

blocks.text: Gmail accounts: IMAP and sign-in settings

If you use Gmail, you have less to fix than you might expect. Google's help page says IMAP access has been on by default in Gmail since January 2025, so you do not need to turn it on. Google recommends Sign in with Google as the safer way to sync mail.

Google also says app passwords aren't recommended and are unnecessary in most cases. If Mail offers Sign in with Google, use it. For more detail on Gmail, read [How to add Gmail to Apple Mail on Mac](/how-to/use-gmail-in-apple-mail-in-gmail).
Check server settings when sign-in fails

Some accounts need you to open the server fields. Go to Mail > Settings, click Accounts, select the account on the left, and click Server Settings. Apple says the fields you see depend on the account type and whether the account is enabled.

items: User Name and Password: the sign-in details for incoming mail.
Host Name: the incoming mail server address your provider gives you.
Automatically manage connection settings: lets Mail choose the settings for you.
Port and Use TLS/SSL: control how Mail connects to the server.
Advanced IMAP or Exchange Settings: includes IMAP Path Prefix, TLS Certificate, and Allow insecure authentication.

blocks.text: Outgoing mail has its own section. It includes Account, User Name, Password, Host Name, and Automatically manage connection settings. The Account option is where you find Edit SMTP Server List, which you use when you need to check or change the outgoing server.

blocks.title: Leave insecure options off
blocks.text: Allow insecure authentication sits in the Advanced IMAP settings. Keep it off unless your provider tells you to turn it on. Turning it on lowers the protection on your sign-in.

blocks.title: Start with automatic settings
blocks.text: Leave Automatically manage connection settings on unless your provider gives you exact values. Typing values by hand adds chances for error.
Common mistakes when adding an account

items: Adding the account before creating it on the provider's website. Apple says to create it there first.
Typing a nickname instead of the full email address.
Choosing iCloud or Exchange for an address that belongs to another provider.
Changing server fields again and again instead of checking them once against the provider's help page.
Removing an account to fix a sign-in error. Removing it deletes the local copies of its messages.

blocks.text: Pause or remove an account without losing mail
To pause an account, go to Mail > Settings > Accounts and clear Enable this account. Mail stops using it, and you can turn it back on later.

Removing an account is the risky step. It deletes the account's messages from this Mac, but copies stay on the mail server. If you want to keep messages on your Mac, move them into an On My Mac mailbox before you remove the account.
iCloud Mail and custom domains

Custom iCloud email domains need a primary iCloud Mail address first. The same Apple Account must be signed in on each device that uses the domain. Check both before you add the custom domain to Mail.
Apple's pages don't compare Mail on Mac with icloud.com. If you are choosing between them, test both with a spare account for a few days before you commit.
Why Apple Mail is worth setting up on a Mac

Litmus, which publishes email client market share data, reports that Apple Mail accounted for 76.56% of email opens in September 2026. That figure comes from more than 1.5 billion opens. It counts opens, not users, and Apple's Mail Privacy Protection inflates Apple's share, so treat it as a rough signal.
Keyboard shortcuts after setup
Once your account works, a few shortcuts save time. These come from Apple's Mail shortcut page. The page does not list a shortcut for Settings or for Add Account, so use the menus for those.

Once the account works, you may want a signature, a rule, or a VIP mailbox. Each one has its own guide on this site.

blocks.text: Which macOS version these steps match

The Apple pages I checked are labeled for macOS 27 Golden Gate. Their version selector also lists Tahoe 26, Sequoia 15, and Sonoma 14. I could not confirm which version the steps were written for, and I found no Tahoe-specific change to adding an account. If a menu name looks different on your Mac, check your macOS version and compare it with Apple's guide for that release.
What to do when sign-in still fails

Apple's pages do not list troubleshooting steps for specific error messages. Start with the password, then check that the account exists on the provider's website. After that, compare the server fields with the values your provider publishes.
If you use Gmail and get a password prompt you didn't expect, go back to Sign in with Google. Google's guidance is to avoid app passwords where you can.

faq.question: Do I need to create the account on the provider's website first?
faq.answer: Yes. Apple says to create the account on the provider's website before you add it in System Settings under Internet Accounts. Doing it first also lets you confirm that your password works.

faq.question: Can I add more than one account to Apple Mail?
faq.answer: Yes. Mail lists each account under Mail > Settings > Accounts. You can pause any one of them by clearing Enable this account.

faq.question: Why doesn't Mail list Yahoo, AOL, or Outlook?
faq.answer: Apple's add-account page lists iCloud, Gmail, Exchange, and school, work, or other accounts. It does not name Yahoo, AOL, or Outlook. For those, try Add Other Account in System Settings > Internet Accounts and check the provider's help page for server values.

faq.question: Will removing an account delete my email?
faq.answer: It deletes the account's messages from this Mac. Copies stay on the mail server. If you want local copies, move messages to an On My Mac mailbox before you remove the account.

faq.question: Do I need an app password for Gmail?
faq.answer: Usually not. Google says app passwords aren't recommended and are unnecessary in most cases. Google also says IMAP has been on by default in Gmail since January 2025. Use Sign in with Google when Mail offers it.

faq.question: Is there a keyboard shortcut for Settings or Add Account?
faq.answer: Apple's keyboard shortcut page does not list one for either. Open the Mail menu and choose Settings or Add Account.

faq.question: Do these steps work on Tahoe or Sequoia?
faq.answer: The Apple pages I checked are labeled for macOS 27, and their selector also lists Tahoe 26, Sequoia 15, and Sonoma 14. I found no Tahoe-specific change. Menu names may differ slightly on older versions, so compare with your own Mac.

appliesTo: Apple Mail on Mac, steps from Apple's macOS 27 guide

steps.name: Open the Mail app
steps.text: Open Mail from the Dock or from the Applications folder. Wait for the main window to appear before you go to the menu bar.
steps.tip: Mail must be the active app, or the menu bar shows the app you are in instead.

steps.name: Choose Add Account
steps.text: Click Mail in the menu bar, then click Add Account. Mail opens a window that asks for an email address. This is the path Apple's Get Started guide uses.
steps.tip: Apple's keyboard shortcut list has no shortcut for this command, so the menu is the way in.

steps.name: Enter your email address
steps.text: Type your full email address, for example name@example.com, and then click Continue.
steps.tip: Use the full address, not a nickname.

steps.name: Or choose from a list
steps.text: If Mail doesn't recognize your address, click choose from a list. Select your provider or domain from the list, then click Continue.
steps.tip: Pick the provider your address belongs to, not the one you wish you had.

steps.name: Follow the on-screen instructions
steps.text: Mail moves to the next screen. Read each prompt, enter the account information it asks for, and continue through the screens. Apple describes this part as following the instructions to enter account information.
steps.tip: Have your password ready. Check it on the provider's website if sign-in fails.

steps.name: Confirm the account in Settings
steps.text: Click Mail, then Settings, then Accounts. Select the new account on the left to confirm it appears and is enabled.
steps.tip: If the account isn't there, return to Add Account and repeat the steps.

steps.name: Open Server Settings only if needed
steps.text: Select the account and click Server Settings when Mail can't connect. Apple notes that the fields you see depend on the account type and whether the account is enabled.
steps.tip: If sign-in already works, leave these fields alone.

steps.name: Check incoming and outgoing servers
steps.text: Compare User Name, Host Name, Port, and Use TLS/SSL with your provider's help page. Keep Automatically manage connection settings on unless the provider gives you exact values.
steps.tip: Leave Allow insecure authentication off unless your provider tells you to change it.

steps.name: Send a test message and get new mail
steps.text: Send a message to another account you control, then check that it arrives. Use the shortcut to get new emails and confirm your inbox loads.
steps.tip: Apple lists ⇧⌘N for Get new emails on its Mail shortcut page.

troubleshooting.problem: Sign-in keeps failing even with the right password
troubleshooting.fix: Check that the account exists on the provider's website, since Apple says to create it there first. For Gmail, use Sign in with Google instead of an app password.
Click choose from a list, or use Add Other Account in System Settings > Internet Accounts. Apple's page names only iCloud, Gmail, Exchange, and school, work, or other accounts.

troubleshooting.problem: Mail can't connect to the server
troubleshooting.fix: Open Mail > Settings > Accounts, select the account, and click Server Settings. Compare Host Name, Port, and Use TLS/SSL with your provider's help page.

troubleshooting.problem: Messages disappeared from this Mac after removing an account
troubleshooting.fix: Removing an account deletes its messages from this Mac, but copies stay on the mail server. Move messages to On My Mac before you remove an account next time.

troubleshooting.problem: The menus don't match these steps
troubleshooting.fix: Apple's pages are labeled for macOS 27 Golden Gate. Check your macOS version and compare it with Apple's guide for that release before you assume something is wrong.
